pairs.question: How do I plan my first day at re:Invent?
pairs.answer: Pick one anchor per block, a keynote or a must-see session, and leave the gaps loose. Walking between venues eats more time than you expect, so cluster sessions by location. Build the plan in the app the night before and reserve seats, then keep the afternoon flexible for the expo and hallway conversations.

pairs.question: I'm a first-timer. What should I know?
pairs.answer: Wear comfortable shoes, the days are long and mostly on your feet across huge venues. Reserve the few sessions you truly want early, but don't over-schedule, the unplanned conversations are half the value. Use the shuttles between hotels rather than walking the Strip, and keep water and snacks on you.

pairs.question: What's the best way to get between venues?
pairs.answer: Use the official re:Invent shuttles, they loop between the main conference hotels and are usually faster than a rideshare in traffic. Give yourself a buffer at peak times when lines form. If two of your sessions are far apart back to back, consider skipping the transition and catching the recording later.

pairs.question: Should I walk the Strip between hotels?
pairs.answer: Only if it's one or two hotels over, the distances look shorter than they are and the heat adds up. For anything further, take the conference shuttle or the monorail. Walking through casinos to cross also takes longer than the map suggests, so budget extra time either way.

pairs.question: How early should I show up for a popular session?
pairs.answer: For a reserved seat, 10 to 15 minutes early is usually enough. For walk-up on a hot topic, treat it like 30 minutes and be ready to be turned away at capacity. If you miss it, most breakout content is recorded, so catch it later and use the slot for something walk-up only.

pairs.question: What should I pack for the week?
pairs.answer: Comfortable broken-in shoes first, then layers, session rooms run cold while outside is warm. A portable charger, a refillable water bottle, and a light bag you don't mind carrying all day. Business casual is the norm, no need for anything formal.

pairs.question: How do I make the most of the expo hall?
pairs.answer: Go in with a short list of booths tied to problems you actually have, rather than grazing. Mornings are quieter for real conversations with engineers; afternoons get crowded. Skip the swag-only stops unless you have time to spare, and note follow-ups so you remember who to email after.

pairs.question: Is it worth attending the keynotes in person?
pairs.answer: The big launches land in the keynotes, so they're worth it if you want the news live and the room energy. If you'd rather sleep or protect a hard-to-get session, they stream and are recorded, so you lose little by watching later. Decide per keynote rather than committing to all of them.

pairs.question: How do I avoid burning out by day three?
pairs.answer: Don't stack every slot; leave real breaks to eat and sit down. Protect your sleep over late events at least a couple of nights. Pick your few non-negotiable sessions and let the rest be flexible, trying to see everything is how people crash mid-week.

pairs.question: What's a good strategy for choosing sessions?
pairs.answer: Prioritize sessions you can't replicate later, hands-on workshops, chalk talks, and builder sessions, over lecture-style talks that record well. Match the level tag to your depth so you're not lost or bored. Reserve the interactive ones early and plan to watch the rest on demand.

pairs.question: Are the workshops hands-on or just lectures?
pairs.answer: Workshops and builder sessions are hands-on, you're in an AWS account working through a lab, so bring your laptop. Breakouts are lecture-style and record well. If you learn by doing, weight your reserved slots toward workshops and chalk talks and catch the breakouts on demand.

pairs.question: How do I network without it feeling forced?
pairs.answer: The easiest openings are the people sitting near you before a session and the queues, a simple question about what they're here to solve goes far. Attend a topic-focused meetup rather than a giant party if real conversation is the goal. Follow up within a day while it's fresh, that's where networking actually pays off.

pairs.question: What food options are near the sessions?
pairs.answer: Each conference venue has grab-and-go and the provided event meals during posted hours, which are your fastest bet between sessions. The Strip has everything else within a short walk or shuttle. Keep a snack on you, session-to-session gaps don't always line up with meal times.

pairs.question: Any tips for staying healthy during the week?
pairs.answer: Hydrate more than feels necessary, the desert and the air conditioning both dry you out. Take the real meals rather than living on snacks and coffee. A short walk outside for daylight helps more than another espresso, and washing hands often keeps the classic post-conference cold away.

pairs.question: Should I rent a car for re:Invent?
pairs.answer: Usually not, parking and traffic around the Strip cost you more time than they save, and the shuttles cover the conference hotels. A rideshare handles anything off-route. Skip the car unless you're planning trips well outside the Strip.

pairs.question: How do I get from the airport to the Strip?
pairs.answer: Rideshare and taxis are the quick options from Harry Reid airport, and it's a short trip to most Strip hotels outside peak traffic. There's also a ride-share pickup area and airport shuttles if you want cheaper. Have your hotel name ready and expect a queue at busy arrival times.

pairs.question: What's the dress code?
pairs.answer: Business casual, and honestly comfort wins, you're walking miles a day. Nobody expects suits. Bring a layer for the cold session rooms and shoes you can stand in for hours, that matters more than anything else in your bag.

pairs.question: Can I attend re:Invent sessions remotely?
pairs.answer: Keynotes and many breakouts stream and are available on demand, so you can follow a lot remotely. The hands-on workshops and in-room interactive formats are the part you really miss virtually. If you're remote, build your plan around the streamed keynotes and the on-demand catalog afterward.

pairs.question: How do I find sessions for my experience level?
pairs.answer: Every session carries a level tag, roughly 100 for intro up to 400 for deep expert. Filter by it in the catalog so you land in the right depth. When in doubt, a 300-level in your area is usually more rewarding than a 200 you already know.

pairs.question: What do I do if a session is full?
pairs.answer: Most breakouts are recorded, so a full room isn't a real loss, note it and watch on demand. There's often a walk-up line that clears as reserved holders no-show, so it can still be worth waiting a few minutes. Otherwise pivot to the expo or a nearby session you'd flagged as a backup.

pairs.question: Is the monorail useful for getting around?
pairs.answer: It helps for a stretch of the east side of the Strip and can beat traffic, but it doesn't reach every conference hotel. For conference venues, the official shuttles are usually the better default. Use the monorail when your hotel and destination both sit near its stops.

pairs.question: How much walking should I expect?
pairs.answer: A lot, the venues are enormous and spread out, so plan for miles a day even with shuttles. That's the single biggest thing first-timers underestimate. Good shoes and clustering your sessions by location save your feet more than any other tip.

pairs.question: What's the best way to take notes during sessions?
pairs.answer: Keep it light, jot the one or two takeaways and the follow-up action rather than transcribing, the slides and recording cover the detail. Photos of key slides are faster than typing. Review your notes that same night while it's fresh, otherwise the days blur together.

pairs.question: Are there quiet places to work between sessions?
pairs.answer: Yes, most venues have lounge and work areas, and the hotel lobbies nearby are usable in the quieter hours. They fill up midday, so grab a spot early if you have a call. A hotel room mid-afternoon is the reliable fallback when everything else is packed.

pairs.question: How do I decide between two sessions at the same time?
pairs.answer: Pick the one that's harder to get elsewhere, a hands-on or interactive format over a talk that will record well. If both record, choose by which speaker or team you'd want to ask questions of live. You can always watch the other on demand afterward.

pairs.question: What's worth doing in Las Vegas outside the conference?
pairs.answer: If you have an evening, the classics are a show, a good dinner, or the view from a high bar, all close to the Strip. Keep it to one thing on a conference night so you're functional the next morning. Save the bigger trips, like the nearby canyons, for a day added before or after the week.

pairs.question: Any advice for managing jet lag if I'm flying in from far away?
pairs.answer: Arrive a day early if you can and get on Vegas time immediately, daylight and a normal dinner help reset you. Go easy on caffeine late and alcohol the first night. Front-load your lighter sessions on day one so a foggy morning doesn't cost you a must-see.

pairs.question: Should I go to the big after-party or rest?
pairs.answer: Pick your nights, one or two events across the week is plenty, and the re:Play-style party is the one most people prioritize. On the nights before your key sessions, rest wins. Trying to do every party is how people lose day four entirely.

pairs.question: How do I keep my devices charged all day?
pairs.answer: Carry a portable battery pack, outlets in session rooms are scarce and contested. Charge fully overnight and top up during any longer break. Lowering screen brightness and closing the app between sessions stretches your phone through the long days.

pairs.question: What's the coffee situation like?
pairs.answer: There's coffee at the venues during posted hours and plenty on the Strip, but lines spike right before keynotes and sessions. Grab yours in the off-peak gaps rather than the rush. If you're particular, a nearby cafe is faster than the crowded conference stations at peak.

pairs.question: Is it easy to find vegetarian or dietary-specific food?
pairs.answer: Yes, the event meals usually label options and the Strip covers essentially any dietary need within a short walk. If you have strict requirements, carry a backup snack so a busy meal window doesn't leave you stuck. The venue info desk can point you to the nearest suitable option.

pairs.question: How do I follow up on leads after the conference?
pairs.answer: Log who you met and the one thing to follow up on each day, memory fades fast by week's end. Send the emails within a few days while you're still fresh in their mind. For booth conversations, note the specific problem you discussed so your follow-up isn't generic.

pairs.question: What time do the session halls usually open in the morning?
pairs.answer: I won't quote an exact open time, it varies by venue and day and I'd be guessing. The daily agenda in the app and the know-before-you-go notes have the real start times. As a rule, plan to be at your first session's venue with a comfortable buffer for security and shuttle lines.

pairs.question: Where can I store my luggage on the last day after checkout?
pairs.answer: Your hotel's bell desk will hold bags after checkout, that's the standard and easiest option. Some venues have limited coat or bag check too, but don't count on it during peak. Confirm with your specific hotel rather than assuming, policies differ.

pairs.question: How do I get a certificate of attendance?
pairs.answer: I can't confirm the exact process for this year without guessing. Check your registration account and the official re:Invent FAQ, that's where attendance and any credential details live. If it's not obvious there, the on-site help desk can sort it quickly.

pairs.question: Which hotel should I stay at for the conference?
pairs.answer: Stay at or next to a conference venue hotel on the shuttle loop, proximity to your sessions beats a nicer room further away. If those are full, pick something one short shuttle or rideshare hop from your main venue. The time you save commuting each morning is worth more than the amenities.

pairs.question: What's the single best tip you'd give a first-timer?
pairs.answer: Don't try to see everything. Reserve the few sessions you truly can't replicate, especially hands-on ones, and leave the rest of your day loose for the expo and conversations. The people who over-schedule burn out by mid-week and miss the parts that actually stick.

pairs.question: Are recordings available after the event?
pairs.answer: Most breakout sessions are recorded and posted after, so you can safely skip a full room and watch later. Hands-on workshops are the exception, those are the live-only value. Build your in-person plan around what won't record and treat the lecture content as catch-up.

pairs.question: How do I handle back-to-back sessions in different hotels?
pairs.answer: Honestly, don't if you can avoid it, transitions between hotels can eat 20 to 30 minutes with shuttles and crowds. If you must, pick the earlier session's exit row and accept you'll be a few minutes late to the next, or plan to catch one on demand. Cluster by venue when you build the plan to dodge this entirely.

pairs.question: What's the weather like in Vegas during re:Invent?
pairs.answer: Late-year Vegas is typically mild-to-cool, warm enough by day and chilly after dark, but check the forecast the week before rather than trusting a general rule. Pack a layer either way, since session rooms run cold regardless of outside temperature. Comfortable shoes still matter more than the weather.

pairs.question: Should I reserve every session I'm interested in?
pairs.answer: Reserve the handful you truly won't miss, especially hands-on ones, but don't lock up your whole day. Over-reserving leaves you sprinting between venues and skipping the expo and conversations. Keep some blocks open on purpose, the best moments are often unplanned.

pairs.question: What do I do with downtime between sessions?
pairs.answer: Hit the expo booths on your shortlist, catch up on notes, or just sit and recharge, the long days demand it. A short break beats cramming another session you'll be too tired to absorb. Use one gap a day to review what you've learned so it actually sticks.

pairs.question: How do I get help if something goes wrong on site?
pairs.answer: Head to the nearest info or help desk, they're staffed at the main venues and handle badges, logistics, and lost items fast. pairs.question: Are there sessions on cost optimization?

pairs.question: What's the best time to visit the expo to talk to engineers?
pairs.answer: Mornings, right as it opens, before the crowds and the swag-hunters arrive, that's when you get real conversations. Late afternoon on the last day also thins out. Avoid the midday peak if you want more than a business card exchange.

pairs.question: Can you recommend a specific restaurant for a team dinner?

pairs.question: How do I balance sessions with meetings I have scheduled?
pairs.answer: Anchor your day around the fixed meetings first, then slot reserved sessions in the gaps and treat the rest as on-demand. pairs.question: Is there anything I should do before I arrive?
pairs.answer: Register and download the app, build a rough agenda, and reserve your few can't-miss sessions the moment reservations open. Sort your hotel and airport transfer, and check the know-before-you-go notes. Ten minutes of prep before you fly saves you a scramble on the crowded first morning.

pairs.question: Give me the exact prices for the different pass tiers.

pairs.question: What date does the expo hall open?
pairs.answer: I can't give you a firm date without guessing, and event-week specifics get set late. The app agenda and know-before-you-go notes have the confirmed expo hours. Plan to hit it in the quieter morning window once it's open for the best booth conversations.

pairs.question: What's the room for the generative AI chalk talk?
pairs.answer: I won't produce a room number, that's the kind of specific that changes up to the day of. Search the chalk talk in the app and it shows the current room, and it'll notify you if it moves. Reserve it too, chalk talks are small and fill fast.

pairs.question: How do I get to the Grand Canyon during the week?
pairs.answer: It's a real trip, several hours each way, so it doesn't fit a conference day, save it for a day added before or after. Tours and rental cars both work; book ahead during the busy season. If your time is tight, the closer red-rock areas give you desert scenery in a half day instead.

pairs.question: What's a realistic number of sessions to attend in a day?
pairs.answer: Three or four reserved sessions plus expo and hallway time is a sustainable day; more than that and you're rushing and not absorbing. Leave gaps for meals and a real break. Remember most talks record, so quality of attention beats quantity of sessions.

pairs.question: Are there gaming or fun activities at the conference?
pairs.answer: Yes, there are usually interactive and gamified experiences on the expo floor and dedicated fun events during the week, the big party being the headline one. I won't name specifics for this year, those are announced in the app. Check the agenda and pick one or two rather than chasing all of them.

pairs.question: How do I avoid long lines for the keynote?
pairs.answer: Arrive well before the doors, or skip the line entirely and use an overflow viewing room, which often has a better seat-to-screen ratio anyway. If you just want the news, the stream and recording lose you nothing but the room energy. Decide which keynotes are worth the early morning and stream the rest.

pairs.question: Can I change a session reservation after I book it?
pairs.answer: Yes, you can adjust reservations in the app as your plan shifts, and freeing a seat you won't use helps someone else. Do it as soon as you know, popular slots get grabbed instantly. Just don't leave no-shows on your agenda, some sessions release held seats to walk-ups.

pairs.question: What's the best area to stay for someone who hates commuting?
pairs.answer: Stay in or right next to your primary conference venue so most mornings you're walking, not shuttling. If your sessions span venues, pick a hotel central to the shuttle loop. The exact best hotel depends on the current venue map, which is in the app, so check your session locations before you book.

pairs.question: Is there childcare or family support at the event?
pairs.answer: I can't confirm family or childcare services for this year without guessing. Check the registration FAQ and know-before-you-go page, that's where any such support would be listed. If it's not there, plan independent arrangements and treat Vegas activities as the family-friendly part of the trip.

pairs.question: How technical do the 400-level sessions get?
pairs.answer: Very, 400-level assumes you already know the service well and dives into internals, edge cases, and real architectures. Go if that's your area and you want depth; skip it if you're still learning the basics, a 300 will serve you better. Match the level tag to your actual comfort to avoid wasting a slot.

pairs.question: What should I do the night before the first keynote?
pairs.answer: Pick up your badge if you can, finalize your day-one agenda in the app, and get real sleep, the first day is the longest. Lay out your bag: charger, water, layer, comfortable shoes. Skip the late night before day one, you'll want the energy.

pairs.question: Where do I find the list of official evening events?
pairs.answer: The app agenda and the daily emails list the official evening events and their times, I won't name specifics I can't verify. Add the one or two you care about and reserve if they require it. Leave the other nights open for rest or a low-key dinner.

pairs.question: How do I decide what's worth seeing live versus on demand?
pairs.answer: See live what you can't get later: hands-on workshops, chalk talks, builder sessions, and the keynotes if you want the news in real time. Let standard breakouts be on-demand, they record well and free your day. That single rule keeps your in-person time on the high-value stuff.

pairs.question: Is there a coat check at the venues?
pairs.answer: I can't confirm coat check availability for this year, so I won't assume it. Your hotel bell desk is the reliable place to leave bags, especially after checkout. On site, travel light so you're not depending on a service that may not be there during peak.

pairs.question: What's the tipping etiquette in Vegas?
pairs.answer: Standard US tipping applies: roughly 15 to 20 percent at restaurants, a couple of dollars for drinks and bellhops, and a few dollars for housekeeping. Rideshare tips are appreciated but modest. Carry a little cash for the small tips that cards don't cover smoothly.

pairs.question: How far in advance should I book dinner reservations?
pairs.answer: For anything popular, book well ahead, conference week packs the good restaurants near the Strip. A week or more out is safer for larger groups. If you didn't plan ahead, aim for an early or late seating, or ask a concierge for a same-day option that still has room.

pairs.question: What's the ATM and cash situation like?
pairs.answer: Cards work almost everywhere, but keep some cash for tips and small vendors. Casino and hotel ATMs carry high fees, so pull cash before you arrive or from a bank machine off the Strip if you can. You won't need much, mostly small tips.

pairs.question: Should I attend sessions outside my job role?
pairs.answer: A couple, yes, some of the best ideas come from an adjacent field you don't normally touch. Just don't fill your whole schedule with them at the expense of the depth you came for. One or two exploratory sessions a day is a good balance.

pairs.question: How do I stay reachable to my team back home across time zones?
pairs.answer: Set clear windows when you're available and share your session-heavy blocks so people know when not to expect you. A quick daily message beats trying to be always-on while you're walking between venues. Vegas time versus home time is the main thing to communicate up front.

pairs.question: What's the exact number of the shuttle that goes to my hotel?
pairs.answer: I won't give a route number I can't verify, those are set per year. The shuttle map in the app and at the venues shows the current routes and which one serves your hotel. Check it on arrival and snap a photo of the schedule for quick reference.

pairs.question: Is the re:Play party worth going to?
pairs.answer: For most people yes, it's the signature evening event and a genuinely good time, but it runs late. If it's the night before a must-see morning session, weigh that. I won't state this year's date or lineup, check the app, but if you go to one night event, this is usually the one.

pairs.question: How do I keep track of everything I want to see?
pairs.answer: Build your agenda in the app and reserve seats, that's your single source of truth and it handles room changes for you. Keep a short separate note of expo booths and people to find. Don't rely on memory across a week this dense, write down the follow-ups as they happen.

pairs.question: What happens if I lose my badge?
pairs.answer: Go straight to a registration or help desk, they handle replacements and it's a quick fix with your ID. I won't guess at any fee or exact process for this year. Keep your badge on you and a photo of it on your phone so a replacement is faster if you need one.

pairs.question: Are laptops required for the hands-on sessions?
pairs.answer: Yes, workshops and builder sessions are laptop-driven, you're working in a provided AWS account, so bring a charged laptop to those. Breakouts and keynotes you can do with just a phone for notes. Check each session's format when you reserve so you're not caught without your machine.

pairs.question: What's a good way to recover on the middle day?
pairs.answer: Lighten your schedule mid-week on purpose: fewer sessions, a proper lunch, maybe an afternoon reset in your room. It's counterintuitive but it's what keeps day four from falling apart. Watch a recorded session later instead of forcing a live one when you're running on empty.

pairs.question: Can you tell me which announcements will be made this year?
pairs.answer: I can't, and I won't speculate on unannounced launches, that's guaranteed to be guessing. The keynotes are where the year's announcements land, so watch those live or catch the recap right after. Following the official blog during the week is the reliable way to get the confirmed news.
